prompt: In 500 words, discuss how contemporary Aristotelian scholars—Nussbaum in particular—interpret the role of phantasia in animal action. Focus on the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit (De Anima III.9-11, De Motu Animalium 6-8), Nussbaum's reading of phantasia as "seeing-as" that supplies motivating content, and any contested points where her reading diverges from e.g. Wedin or the Uexküll biosemiotic analogue of phantasma/Merkbild.

## 1. Nussbaum's influential reading foregrounds precisely this intermediary status, arguing that phantasia is best understood not as a faculty of image-production in the modern sense of "imagination," but rather as a mode of "seeing-as" that supplies the motivating content upon which desire and locomotion depend., "phantasia and desire are jointly necessary conditions for animal motion," and furthermore, "phantasia is a necessary condition for desire," which it must "prepare" before any appetitive movement can be initiated (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 10). This formulation is significant because it establishes phantasia not as a peripheral or derivative cognitive event, but as a structurally prior condition for the entire chain of animal action—what we may call the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit that Aristotle develops across *De Anima* III.9–11 and the *De Motu Animalium*. Indeed, the difficulty of interpreting phantasia arises in part from its resistance to assimilation into any single cognitive category. Aristotle himself distinguishes phantasia from perception (aisthesis), from belief (doxa), and from knowledge (episteme), yet he insists upon its intimate connection with all three. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in his discussion of deliberative capacities, "Sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). This passage establishes the critical internal distinction within phantasia itself: sensitive phantasia (αἰσθητικὴ φαντασία), which belongs to all animals capable of perception, and deliberative or calculative phantasia (λογιστικὴ ἢ βουλευτικὴ φαντασία), which belongs only to rational beings capable of comparing and measuring future possibilities against one another. Nussbaum's reading takes this distinction seriously but focuses primarily on the more basic, sensitive grade of phantasia as the one most relevant to explaining animal locomotion as such—the grade that obtains even in creatures incapable of deliberation. Furthermore, Nussbaum emphasizes that phantasia possesses a degree of voluntariness and activity that passive perception does not., "it is because of the passive character of Aristotelian aisthesis that a further faculty is required agent's selective" engagement with its environment (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47). The phantasizing agent actively retains, reorganizes, and presents sensory residues in a manner that shapes desire; accordingly, phantasia is not merely an afterimage or echo of sensation, but something that the animal does with or upon its perceptual inheritance. This active dimension—the capacity to hold an appearance before the soul even "in the absence of the object" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 39)—is what allows phantasia to serve as the bridge between the world as perceived and the world as desired. 

## 2. Nussbaum on Orexis: Desire (ὄρεξις) If phantasia provides the representational content—the appearing of something as pleasant, painful, fearful, or beneficial—then orexis (desire) constitutes the motive force that translates that content into a directional impulse toward or away from the object so represented. Nussbaum's reading of the *De Motu Animalium* and *De Anima* III.9–11 insists that desire is never self-originating in Aristotle's account; it is always desire for something appearing as something, and it is phantasia that furnishes this appearance. Thus the explanatory order runs from phantasia to orexis, and subsequently from orexis to kinesis. Nussbaum makes this architecture explicit when phantasia "is said to have two sources: sense-perception or thinking," and that "the being (the einai) of phantasia is different from the being of any other faculty, but that phantasia might still be 'the same as' some other faculty" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24). What this suggests is that phantasia's identity is functional rather than ontological in a strict sense; it is individuated by what it does in the economy of action—namely, preparing desire—rather than by a discrete material substrate. Aristotle's own treatment in the *Movement of Animals* reinforces this point. "from the point of view of the account which gives the cause of movement desire is the middle, and desire moves being moved" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, pp. 9–11). Desire, accordingly, occupies a middle position in the causal chain: it is itself moved by the phantasma (the appearing content) and in turn moves the body. Desire is thus simultaneously passive and active—passive insofar as it is aroused and directed by the phantasia, active insofar as it initiates locomotion. This double character is what Nussbaum identifies as the peculiar explanatory richness of Aristotle's model: the animal is neither a passive automaton driven by stimuli nor a purely rational agent deliberating over propositions, but rather a being whose movements are governed by how things appear to it, where that appearing is itself shaped by the totality of involvements constituting its perceptual life. Heidegger's reading of Aristotelian πάθος lends further support to this interpretation; he characterizes the perceptual dimension as "πάσχειν, affected by beings as world; πάσχειν as δέχεσθαι, 'to perceive' and that primarily as πάθος, 'becoming-affected,' 'disposition,' being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). Hence, desire does not arise in a vacuum but from within a disposed, affected being whose world is already structured by phantasia. Similarly, Nussbaum's insistence that phantasia must "prepare" desire underscores that orexis is downstream from a representational activity that is itself shaped by the animal's sensory history and its current mode of attentiveness (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 10). 

## 3. Nussbaum on Kinesis: Movement/Change (κίνησις) The culminating moment of the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit is locomotive movement itself—the bodily change by which an animal pursues or flees the object represented in phantasia and desired or feared through orexis. For Nussbaum, the critical insight is that Aristotle's explanation of kinesis is irreducibly psychological; it is not sufficient to describe the mechanical articulation of limbs or the physiological transmission of heat and cold—one must also account for the representational and appetitive conditions without which no locomotion would be intelligible as action. She stresses that Aristotle links "noesis and phantasia in an account of physiological alterations," suggesting that in a living body "the activities of nous must be linked with those of the faculty of phantasia, which it would not be implausible to see as realized in some physiological occurrences" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 26–27). This passage illuminates the dual-aspect character of Aristotelian kinesis: the movement is at once a physiological event (an alteration in the bodily organs, a kinesis in the strict sense) and a psychologically structured event (an action undertaken in light of a phantasma). Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle's concept of movement provides a complementary philosophical framework here. "movement is not a being, but a how of being-there, such that the how of this there is something already present: look" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 266). This formulation—kinesis as a "how of being-there" rather than a freestanding entity—resonates deeply with Nussbaum's emphasis on the irreducibility of the psychological dimension. If movement is a mode of being-there rather than a substance, then its intelligibility requires reference to the total situation of the moving being, including its perceptual and appetitive orientation. Furthermore, Heidegger's reading of ἐνέργεια and its relation to κίνησις clarifies the ontological stakes: "it happened that the name ἐνέργεια also came to be carried over to the other, to what contrasted with determinations of movement; ἐνέργεια, specifically, is related in itself πρὸς τὴν ἐντελέχειαν" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 213–215). Thus the passage from potentiality to actuality that constitutes kinesis is also a passage toward ἐντελέχεια—toward the realization of the animal's form in its fullest expression. For Nussbaum, accordingly, the practical syllogism that structures animal action (the phantasma as minor premise, the general desire as major premise, the action as conclusion) is not an abstract logical schema imposed upon behavior, but a description of how the animal's being-there moves from appearance through desire to actualized movement. Indeed, Aristotle's account of how "one calculates, using the phantasmata or noëmata in the soul, as if one saw the things, and plans for the future in view of the present" illustrates the way in which deliberative phantasia mediates between temporal horizons in the service of kinesis (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). 

## 4. Nussbaum and the Biosemiotic Parallel The structural parallel between Aristotle's phantasma and Jakob von Uexküll's concept of the Merkbild—the "perceptual image" or "recognition mark" that an organism carries within itself as a guide to action—constitutes one of the most productive cross-textual bridges available for contemporary scholarship on animal cognition. Both the phantasma and the Merkbild are organism-internal perceptual residues that guide action in the absence of current stimulation; both function not as copies of an objective external world but as selective, species-specific representations shaped by the organism's characteristic mode of engagement with its environment., "every animal is a subject, which, in virtue of the structure peculiar to it, selects stimuli from the general influences of the outer world, and to these it responds in a certain way" (von Uexküll, *Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans*, p. 42). This formulation aligns remarkably with Nussbaum's reading of phantasia as "seeing-as"—a selective, interpretive engagement with the perceptual field that is irreducible to passive reception. Nussbaum's phantasia produces motions (kinēseis) in the living creature "which persist in the absence of the object" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 39). Subsequently, these residual motions function to prepare desire and orient the animal's locomotion even when the original sensory stimulus is no longer present. This is precisely the function of the Merkbild in Uexküll's biosemiotic framework: the organism does not merely react to present stimuli but carries within itself a structured image that enables recognition, anticipation, and appropriate behavioral response. The phantasma, like the Merkbild, is thus a semiotic entity—a sign within the organism's internal economy that mediates between perception and action, between world and movement. 

## 5. Nussbaum and the Merkbild While the preceding section established the structural homology between phantasma and Merkbild at a general level, it is essential to attend more carefully to the points of divergence and interpretive tension that arise when these two frameworks are set alongside one another. Nussbaum's reading, grounded in the Aristotelian text, treats phantasia as a faculty belonging to the soul—a psychic capacity defined by its functional role within the explanatory architecture of De Anima and the De Motu Animalium. By contrast, Uexküll's Merkbild is embedded within a thoroughgoing biological semiotics that resists the hylomorphic vocabulary of form and matter, actuality and potentiality. Von Uexküll insists that "the environments of animals are by no means a part of the environment that opens up to us as human observers; rather, they are the products of the subject itself" (von Uexküll, *Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans*, p. 53). This claim gestures toward a constructivist epistemology that perhaps goes further than Aristotle's own account; for Aristotle, the phantasma retains a causal connection to the external sensible object, even if its persistence and active deployment by the animal introduce a measure of autonomy from that origin. However, Nussbaum's emphasis on the active and selective character of phantasia brings the Aristotelian position closer to Uexküll's constructivism than a purely causal reading would suggest., the "passive character of Aristotelian aisthesis" necessitates "a further faculty" to account for the animal's selective engagement with its surroundings (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47). It is perhaps in this selectivity—this capacity to retain certain appearances and not others, to present certain features of the environment as salient while allowing others to recede—that the deepest convergence between phantasma and Merkbild is to be found. Heidegger's characterization of the perceiving being as "being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it" further illuminates this convergence, suggesting that the organism's perceptual life is always already a mode of practical engagement rather than a neutral registration of stimuli (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). Wedin's more conservative reading, by contrast, would resist this rapprochement, insisting on the causal derivation of phantasia from actual sensation and thus limiting its constructive or interpretive scope. The tension between these readings—between phantasia as causally derived kinesis and phantasia as functionally autonomous perceptual interpretation—remains productively unresolved in the literature, and it is precisely at this point that the biosemiotic analogy proves most illuminating, since Uexküll's Merkbild is similarly both causally dependent upon sensory encounter and functionally autonomous in guiding subsequent behavior. Accordingly, the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit that Nussbaum identifies at the heart of Aristotle's theory of action finds a compelling, if not exact, structural analogue in the Uexküllian functional circle (Funktionskreis), where Merkbild and Wirkbild together constitute the organism's active relation to its environment. What Nussbaum's reading thus enables is a recognition that Aristotle's account of animal action already contains, in nascent form, the biosemiotic insight that perception and action are not separable moments but constitute a unified circuit of organismic engagement with a meaningful world. --- # VALIDATION APPENDIX ## Claim Map | # | Claim | Source | Page(s) |
